title: Connecting the API to MongoDB
summary: Use the official Node.js driver to connect, insert and read, with the connection string kept in an environment variable.

quiz.q: Why should a connection string with a password stay out of your source code?
options: Anyone who sees the code, for example on GitHub, could use your database
Node.js refuses to run files that contain it
MongoDB rejects strings that are written in code
quiz.explain: Code is shared and copied. A secret inside it is shared too. Environment variables keep the secret on the machine that runs the program.

quiz.q: Complete the line that reads the connection string from the environment.
quiz.explain: `process.env` is an object holding the environment variables of the running process.

quiz.q: What does `students.find({})` return in the Node.js driver?
options: A cursor, which you turn into an array with toArray()
quiz.explain: `find` gives a cursor so large results can be read in pieces. Call `await ....toArray()` to get a plain array.

quiz.q: Click the line that will hand back a promise instead of the saved result.
quiz.explain: `insertOne` returns a promise. Without `await` the next line sees the promise, not the result, so `insertedId` is undefined.

exercise.task:
Complete `db.js` with the official driver.

- Import `MongoClient` from `mongodb`.
- Read the connection string from `process.env.MONGODB_URI` (no password written in the file).
- Create a client with `new MongoClient(uri)` and `await client.connect()`.
- Get the `students` collection of the `marks` database.
- Add a student with `insertOne` and read all students with `find({}).toArray()`.
- Close the client with `client.close()`.
hints: Work through the TODO comments in order. Everything after `connect()` needs the `await` keyword.
The collection comes from chaining `client.db('marks').collection('students')`. Pass a student object to `insertOne`.
